newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bosnia conference to back peace consolidation plan.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia conference to back peace consolidation plan.

text.p: Bosnia's three co-presidents and the major powers will adopt a two-year peace consolidation plan for the former Yugoslav republic on Thursday after a flareup of fighting highlighted the fragility of the truce.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette, who will co-chair the Paris meeting with international mediator Carl Bildt, said the aim was to give a new impulse to the civilian peace process a year after the Dayton accords ended the Balkans conflict.

"A number of things are still fragile. That's true for the establishment of joint institutions, which is running late...It is true of the return of refugees, which faces many problems, and it's true for reconstruction, which has barely begun," he told a news conference.

Adding to that list of problems, Serbs and Moslems fought a gun battle over the disputed village of Gajevi in northeastern Bosnia on Tuesday in the worst fighting since the Dayton peace accord was struck. American and Russian soldiers had to separate the sides after a Moslem was killed and four people injured.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher is meeting the three Bosnian co-presidents jointly on Wednesday to press home their responsibility for making sure that the peace and joint institutions agreed at Dayton work in practice, aides said.

De Charette and U.S. officials said the priorities in Paris were to complete Bosnia's institutions, build a functioning market economy, speed the return of refugees displaced by ethnic cleansing and war, and improve civil liberties, including press freedom.

A second conference in London in early December will then adopt an action programme for the next year, by which time NATO is likely to have formally approved a slimmed-down peacekeeping force to succeed the Peace Implementation Force (IFOR), whose mandate expires at the end of the year.

Officials stressed the post-IFOR force was not on the agenda in Paris. France wants the force to be gradually phased out over the two-year consolidation period, while the United States and other allies are only talking about the next 12 months.

A senior U.S. official said the document to be adopted at the Paris steering group meeting involves mutual commitments by the Bosnian leaders, representing the Moslems, Croats and Serbs, and the international community.
"It is important to make sure the substance of a lasting peace is built...to give meat to the Bosnian peace," he said.

The official said Washington was determined to go ahead on what he called a cautious rearming of the Moslem-Croat federation in Bosnia to create a balance of power with the Serbs, whom he accused of not fully declaring their weapons.
One big arms shipment has been frozen until Sarajevo fires Deputy Defence Minister Hasan Cengic, who the U.S. official said was obstructing the creation of joint Moslem-Croat defence structures.
He said Washington expected Cengic to be removed soon, as well as an unnamed Croat official who was also blocking the process of integration.

After Wednesday's intensive preparatory talks, the Thursday conference will be a relatively brief affair, with a three-hour working session to approve a statement of guiding principles, a lunch and a closing ceremony at President Jacques Chirac's Elysee palace.

The countries attending will be Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia and rump Yugoslavia, the United States, Russia, France, Britain, Germany, Italy, Canada, the Netherlands, Ireland as current president of the European Union and Turkey, representing the Islamic Conference Organisation.
Several international organisations will also be represented: the United Nations, the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Euorpe and NATO.
